The question this page answers

Is digital finance becoming durable financial use — or do the available data still mainly measure infrastructure and transactions?

Payments: POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden rose from 561 to 1,473 between March 2025 and January 2026; how many people use them is not measured

Administrative payment data can show devices, accounts, transactions and values at high frequency. They are useful signals about the payment system, but each counts a different object, and none can be turned into a number of people or an inclusion outcome without a documented method.

How numbers are presented

Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment.

Explore questionsOpen evidence
What this does not establish

What payment growth does not establish

More terminals do not prove more unique users. More transactions do not reveal how many people used the service. Nominal transaction value does not show real purchasing-power growth. Accounts, wallet subscribers and registrations are not necessarily active people. A rule, project or new institution is not observed adoption. And successful cash delivery or opening an account is not proof of durable post-transfer use.

What we still do not know

What is still missing to measure use

This resource still lacks a comparable, privacy-safe measure of unique and repeat payment users across providers and rails, with frequency, recency, transaction purpose, failed/abandoned attempts and clear active-use definitions. It also lacks the downstream usage series needed to measure adoption after major payment-rail milestones. The FMIIP results framework itself keeps operational state, participating institutions, use cases, merchant acceptance, active accounts, customer transaction costs and electronic-payment beneficiaries as separate measures; project targets remain targets until they are observed.

03Analysis

POS: three different signals

Within the reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), reported POS terminals rose from 561 to 1,473 between March 2025 and January 2026, transaction counts from 8,015 to 24,026 (after a high of 27,187 in July 2025) and nominal transaction value from YER 320 million to YER 1,262 million. This page keeps these three measures separate. A terminal is infrastructure, a transaction is an event and transaction value is a nominal monetary amount; none equals a person.

04What it means

Before comparing payment numbers, ask what each one counts

Cards, accounts, e-wallet subscribers, POS terminals and transactions count different things. Accounts or subscribers may contain duplication or inactivity; terminals are infrastructure; transactions are events. A people-level inclusion rate requires a documented unique-person method rather than a division of administrative totals by population.

Another view of the evidence
05Evidence

E-wallet subscribers: figures from two reports that do not form one series

The CBY-Aden payments report for the third quarter of 2024 gives e-wallet subscriber counts of 414,631 for Q1, 507,585 for Q2 and 581,075 for Q3. The first-half 2025 infographic reports 2,102,484 subscribers. The two publications' subscriber definitions and reporting scope have not been reconciled, so the 2025 figure is not joined to the 2024 quarters and the difference is not read as growth. A subscriber count is not a count of unique people or of active users, and neither publication measures how many adults use a wallet.

06System context

What FPS and RTGS mean — and what they do not yet prove

The World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) separates three payment-infrastructure jobs. The Fast Payment System (FPS) is the project’s fast electronic-payment component, which the project supports in areas under the internationally recognized government. The Real-Time Gross Settlement system (RTGS), to be managed by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) alongside an upgrade of its core banking system, is the settlement backbone the project links to large-value payments between financial institutions. A third component supports access and use through access-point mapping, capacity building for financial institutions and payment service providers, merchant onboarding in underserved areas and outreach. Separately, CBY-Aden records from 2026 show a board decision on what the source calls a national QR standard and e-wallet interconnection, unified-network integration work, and the establishment and governance of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company (YPCC). These records show what architecture and institutions are being built; they do not by themselves establish go-live, reliability, transaction coverage, active use or inclusion outcomes.

07Analysis

Historical e-money evidence shows why registration cannot be read as durable use

Within a study of five e-money providers by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS), e-money accounts reached 807,919 in December 2019, while the same source reports an average 23% dormant/inactive share and notes that some accounts were used once or because circumstances imposed their use. CauseWay’s reproducible grouping of the source’s 2019 transaction-value table indicates 57.03% cash-in/cash-out, 29.97% movement between bank and electronic accounts, and 2.41% for bills and purchases together. These are historical patterns within the study’s providers, not current national prevalence.

More evidence and context

Evidence

January 2026 was the latest monthly POS release on the CBY-Aden payments page as checked on 26 September 2026

The payments page of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 26 September 2026, publishes monthly POS releases from March 2025 through January 2026. This resource therefore stops the monthly series at January 2026. That does not mean activity stopped; it means no later monthly release had been published on that page when it was checked.

Evidence Readings on this question

Evidence periodProvider data 2016–2019, from a 2020 study of five e-money providers
When does digital growth become durable use?
Historical evidence from Yemen records a large base of e-money accounts by 2019 alongside dormancy, one-off use and a transaction mix still closely tied to cash. The open question is whether people choose to return to digital finance and find enough value to keep using it.
Open this Reading
Evidence periodPOS counts March 2025 – January 2026 · institutional records June–August 2026 · project results framework January 2025
When does a payment reform become financial inclusion?
A rule can be issued, infrastructure can expand, institutions can be created and transactions can appear while evidence on reach, repeated use, service quality, protection and outcomes remains incomplete. The question is how far a reform’s effects can actually be traced.

What measurement would change the decision?

PriorityP0 · Payments / People
Active and repeat digital use
Administrative data show registrations, infrastructure and transactions, while historical evidence also records dormancy and one-time or imposed use; unique repeat users are not measured consistently.
Evidence needed: Provider/rail administrative data with deduplication rules and/or demand-side active-use measures.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would distinguish registration or temporary activity from repeat use, merchant use and sustained financial use.
Open this measurement priority
PriorityP1 · Identity / Digital access
Digital onboarding and identity journeys
KYC and e-money rules are documented, but this resource lacks journey-level evidence on attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost.
Evidence needed: Journey-level administrative or survey data across onboarding stages: identity and KYC verification, attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would identify where users leave or fail the onboarding journey and which frictions are associated with those points.

When was it measured or observed?Mar-2025–Jan-2026
POS infrastructure expanded
POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) rose from 561 in March 2025 to 1,473 in January 2026, within CBY-Aden's reporting scope. The December 2025 total of 1,357 and the January 2026 total of 1,473 imply growth of 8.55%, while the January source graphic displays +11%; the POS terminals chart plots the published totals, the +11% is stated under 'How was it produced?' in this record, and the difference is recorded as an inconsistency within the source.
Who or what does it apply to? POS terminals within the payment-system reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden); how far that scope covers each area of Yemen is not established.
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?No observation period: a measurement rule that applies whenever administrative accounts, subscribers or transactions are compared with survey measures of people.
Accounts and transactions are not unique people
Administrative accounts, e-wallet subscribers and payment transactions are not equivalent to unique people measured by Findex.
Who or what does it apply to? Different units of measurement: administrative accounts, wallet subscribers and transactions versus unique people represented by a population survey.
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?Monthly releases for March 2025 to January 2026; page checked on 26 September 2026
Latest monthly POS release listed by CBY-Aden: January 2026 (page checked 26 September 2026)
The payments page of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists monthly POS releases from March 2025 to January 2026. When the page was checked on 26 September 2026, January 2026 was the latest release listed; no later month is inferred.
Who or what does it apply to? Monthly POS releases on the payments page of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), covering its reporting scope
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?Dec-2019; contextual series 2016–2019
807,919 accounts did not mean 807,919 active people
Within the five e-money providers covered by a study of the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS), electronic-money accounts reached 807,919 in December 2019. The same source reports an average 23% dormant/inactive share and notes that some accounts were used once or because circumstances imposed their use. Registered accounts therefore cannot be read as active or durable inclusion.
Who or what does it apply to? Five electronic-money providers/wallets captured by the study
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?Observations published by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) for the first three quarters of 2024 (subscribers), 2024 Q3, 2025 H1 and September 2025; later official context is kept separately.
Wallet and subscriber counts from different publications are not yet reconciled
Official CBY-Aden publications report different wallet counts at different dates and in different contexts—7 in 2024 Q3, 9 in 2025 H1 and 8 licensed e-wallets in a September 2025 official statement. The 2024 Q3 payments report gives e-wallet subscriber counts of 414,631, 507,585 and 581,075 for the first three quarters of 2024, and the H1 2025 infographic gives 2,102,484 for 2025 H1. Because definitions and reporting scope have not been reconciled across these publications, neither set is presented as a continuous trend, and subscribers are not unique people or active users.
Who or what does it apply to? Wallet/e-wallet provider counts and e-wallet subscriber counts as defined by each cited source of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden); the provider definition, subscriber definition and counting basis may differ by source.
